item.description: arXiv:2611.15618v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Synthetic data augmentation has been proposed as a way to artificially supplement clinical datasets to address fairness concerns in downstream classification algorithms. This approach is closely related to upweighting or upsampling methods employed for the problem of class imbalance, which have shown mixed empirical results in practice. Synthetic data augmentation also runs the risk of overfitting to the noise present in subgroups with relatively small sample sizes, raising both generalizability and transportability concerns. We present an empirical evaluation of synthetic data augmentation for fairness in tabular data using simulation studies as well as a real-world application of in-hospital mortality classification for heart failure patients in two distinct data samples. We implement upsampling and upweighting methods as benchmarks for the implicit fairness objective of synthetic data augmentation. Our results suggest that the fairness impacts of data augmentation are sensitive to the design of the downstream algorithm as well as the deployment context and its similarity to the training data. It is crucial that studies making generalizability and transportability claims should provide empirical support for these assertions.
item.dc:creator: I. Elizabeth Kumar, Sherri Rose

item.title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.15634v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana, Aitor Almeida

item.title: Empirical Bayes mirror testing for persistent widening of achievement gaps in U.S. school districts
item.description: arXiv:2611.15667v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unequal recovery from pandemic learning losses raises concerns about widening achievement gaps between economically disadvantaged students and their peers. This study seeks to identify districts whose mathematics gaps widened in every annual interval from 2022 to 2025. The analysis uses estimates from the Stanford Education Data Archive (SEDA) for 5,600 U.S. school districts. Identifying such districts requires accounting for correlated errors and differing precision in the estimated annual changes, as well as multiplicity. The true annual gap changes in each district form an effect vector, and persistent widening means that every component is positive. To address this class of multiple testing problems, we propose an empirical Bayes mirror procedure. It uses an estimated distribution of effect vectors to guide ranking and covariance-adjusted mirror observations to calibrate selection. The procedure achieves finite-sample false discovery rate (FDR) control under a Gaussian observation model, without requiring accurate estimation of the posterior null probabilities used for ranking. Simulations demonstrate power gains from incorporating information about the distribution of effect vectors. At a target FDR of 25%, the SEDA analysis identifies eight districts in five states with evidence of widening gaps in every annual interval.
item.dc:creator: Bowen Gang, Yin Xia

item.title: Global-Local and Window-Concatenated Functional Random Forests: Early and Late Fusion of Window-Specific Functional Principal Components
item.description: arXiv:2611.15816v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Functional random forests built on a single functional principal component decomposition of the whole domain may dilute features confined to short intervals, whose location is rarely known in advance. We propose two random forests based on window-specific functional principal components. The global-local functional random forest (GL-FRF) is a late-fusion method that stacks a tuned full-curve forest and one forest per window with penalised convex weights; it contains the full-curve forest as a feasible solution, and its weights indicate which parts of the domain drive the prediction. The window-concatenated functional random forest (WC-FRF) is an early-fusion method that trains a single tuned forest on the concatenated window-specific scores. On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest with the same number of trees on 16, with Brier score reductions of up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment. No method was best on more than six datasets. WC-FRF was more accurate than GL-FRF on 13 datasets but failed when the signal required the full curve, whereas GL-FRF had the smallest mean and maximum excess over the best method across all 32 simulated and real settings, which makes it the safer choice when the location of the signal is unknown.
item.dc:creator: Fabrizio Maturo, Annamaria Porreca

item.title: Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss
item.description: arXiv:2611.15829v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model's density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Remy, Raphael Rossellini, Chihway Chang, Rebecca Willett

item.title: Nonsense nonlinear correlations between independent random walks
item.description: arXiv:2611.16614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sample distance correlation can remain large between independent random walks. For centred walks with independent, identically distributed increments of finite, positive variance, we prove convergence in distribution to the distance correlation of the joint occupation measure of two independent Brownian paths. This universal limit lies strictly between zero and one almost surely and has full support on the unit interval. We calculate the expected squared distance covariance of the limiting measure and show that ordinary permutation calibration rejects independence with probability tending to one at every fixed nominal level. Gaussian simulations illustrate the persistent dispersion of random-walk correlations and the failure of permutation calibration.
item.dc:creator: Liping Zhu, Zhongming Xie

item.title: AIDA: Analysis of Interval Data in R
item.description: arXiv:2611.16723v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AIDA is an R package that provides tools for the analysis of interval-valued data, including construction, visualization, robust estimation, and explainable outlier detection. The package is built around the intData class and is designed to support methodological research and applied workflows involving interval-valued data. AIDA implements methods for symbolic covariance estimation based on the Mallows distance, robust estimation via the Interval Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator, and explainable outlier detection using Shapley values. The package also includes visualization tools to support interpretation of the results and several interval-valued datasets.
item.dc:creator: Catarina P. Loureiro, M. Ros\'ario Oliveira, Paula Brito

item.title: Automatic Threshold Selection Leaves Finite-Degree Bias in Network Power-Law Fits
item.description: arXiv:2611.16817v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Minimum-distance fitting selects a degree threshold and a power-law exponent from the same network. We study the procedure that fits a continuous Pareto law with the Hill estimator and minimizes the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance over retained ranks. For homogeneous linear preferential attachment and Norros--Reittu graphs with Pareto weights, we derive the joint limiting law of the selected rank, retained fraction of the threshold tie, and exponent error. The selector retains of order $n^{2/(\alpha+2)}$ of $n$ vertices, where $\alpha$ is the survival exponent. At this rank, integer spacing and finite-degree departures from a Pareto tail have the same order as sampling fluctuations. The exponent estimate is consistent and retains a shift on the scale used for confidence intervals. For integer degree laws whose tail sums have a first-order inverse-degree expansion, adding the retained tie fraction divided by the threshold to the Hill statistic removes the leading contribution of the tie. Under homogeneous preferential attachment with a fixed known number of edges per new vertex, removing the remaining model-specific term and calibrating for selection gives confidence intervals with asymptotically exact coverage. Observed networks show sensitivity of the fitted exponent and the classification of degree variance to threshold ties. Simulations assess interval coverage and show improved pooled connectivity predictions after correction under both specified graph laws. Changes to the Norros--Reittu weight distribution can reverse the prediction gain.
item.dc:creator: Tiandong Wang

item.title: Sticky Manifold Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo for Bayesian Model Averaging
item.description: arXiv:2611.17008v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assigning positive prior probability to lower-dimensional submodels enriches the range of uncertainty that Bayesian models can represent. The resulting posterior distributions combine continuous parameter uncertainty with discrete model uncertainty. Efficient movement between these submodels, however, can be difficult to design. We propose the sticky manifold construction as a principled, modular framework for combining piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) across different submodels. The integration is rejection-free, requires no additional likelihood evaluations, and retains the non-reversible and ballistic nature of the component PDMP dynamics. We prove that the resulting process leaves the intended mixed-dimensional target invariant. We also develop a manifold PDMP algorithm based on coordinate charts to provide the within-submodel dynamics and a blow-up procedure that resolves singular sets into codimension-one sticky boundaries. This geometric construction makes the remaining design choices explicit; component dynamics and unsticking kernels can be chosen freely, subject to easily verifiable velocity compatibility conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the sticky manifold algorithms in Bayesian model averaging examples, propagating uncertainty over pure versus mixed states in quantum state tomography, rank in Bayesian principal component analysis, and parametric families in survival extrapolation.
item.dc:creator: Hirofumi Shiba, Luke Hardcastle, Kengo Kamatani

item.title: A Family-Level Graphical Gatekeeping Procedure with Iterative Retesting
item.description: arXiv:1611.03439v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Confirmatory clinical trials often involve multiple objectives grouped into families according to scientific priorities. At the intersection of graphical multiple testing and gatekeeping methods, we develop a Bonferroni-based family-level graphical procedure with partial-rejection-based transfers and iterative re-testing. Families are tested sequentially within each stage, using fixed component tests and a prespecified transition matrix. The updating rule combines current-stage forward contributions based on current family levels with previous-stage backward contributions based on initial allocations. We establish strong global familywise error rate control at a prespecified level under arbitrary dependence. The construction permits backward feedback while retaining fixed component tests and transition coefficients, distinguishing its implementation from forward-only family-level procedures and the specified superchain algorithm. Simulations demonstrate gains over the corresponding No-retest procedure, while identifying an efficiency cost relative to a hypothesis-level graphical comparator with matched initial allocations and edge weights. Clinical illustrations show how the procedure implements family-level priorities and feedback, and an extension accommodates a two-layer structure with multiple families per layer.
item.dc:creator: Zhiying Qiu, Wenge Guo, Sanat Sarkar

item.title: Semiparametric Copula Estimation for Spatially Correlated Multivariate Mixed Outcomes: Analyzing Visual Sightings of Fin Whales from a Line Transect Survey
item.description: arXiv:2312.12710v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For marine biologists, ascertaining the dependence structures between marine species and marine environments, such as sea surface temperature and ocean depth, is imperative for defining ecosystem functioning and providing insights into the dynamics of marine ecosystems. However, obtained data include not only continuous but also discrete data, such as binaries and counts (referred to as mixed outcomes), as well as spatial correlations, both of which make conventional multivariate analysis tools impractical. To solve this issue, we propose semiparametric Bayesian inference and develop an efficient algorithm for computing the posterior of the dependence structure based on the rank likelihood under a latent multivariate spatial Gaussian process using the Markov chain Monte Carlo method. To alleviate the computational intractability caused by the Gaussian process, we also provide a scalable implementation that leverages the nearest-neighbor Gaussian process. Extensive numerical experiments reveal that the proposed method reliably infers the dependence structures of spatially correlated mixed outcomes. Finally, we apply the proposed method to a dataset collected during an international synoptic krill survey in the Scotia Sea of the Antarctic Peninsula to infer the dependence structure between fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus), krill biomass, and relevant oceanographic data.
item.dc:creator: Tomotaka Momozaki, Tomoyuki Nakagawa, Shonosuke Sugasawa, Hiroko Kato Solvang

item.title: On the modelling and prediction of high-dimensional functional time series
item.description: arXiv:2406.00700v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a two-step procedure to model and predict high-dimensional functional time series, where the number of function-valued time series $p$ is large in relation to the length of time series $n$. Our first step performs an eigenanalysis of a positive definite matrix, which leads to a one-to-one linear transformation for the original high-dimensional functional time series, and the transformed curve series can be segmented into several groups such that any two subseries from any two different groups are uncorrelated both contemporaneously and serially. Consequently in our second step those groups are handled separately without the information loss on the overall linear dynamic structure. The second step is devoted to establishing a finite-dimensional dynamical structure for all the transformed functional time series within each group. Furthermore the finite-dimensional structure is represented by that of a vector time series. Modelling and forecasting for the original high-dimensional functional time series are realized via those for the vector time series in all the groups. We investigate the theoretical properties of our proposed methods, and illustrate the finite-sample performance through both extensive simulation and two real datasets.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Qin Fang, Xinghao Qiao, Qiwei Yao

item.title: A grid-based methodology for fast online changepoint detection
item.description: arXiv:2504.09573v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a grid-based methodology that turns suitable offline (non-sequential) changepoint tests into online (sequential) procedures by testing for changes over a dynamically updating grid of candidate locations. For a broad class of test statistics, including those based on empirical averages and certain likelihood ratios, we show that the resulting online procedure has update and storage costs that grow at most logarithmically with the sample size. We further show that the resulting procedure has explicit control of the false alarm probability, and that finite-sample power guarantees for the test translate directly into non-asymptotic upper bounds on the detection delay, provided the test is robust to constant-factor misspecification of the changepoint location. We illustrate the methodology by constructing online detectors for changes in the mean and in the covariance matrix of multivariate data, and prove that their detection delays are near-optimal. The effectiveness of the methodology is supported by a simulation study, where we compare its performance in detecting mean changes with that of state-of-the-art online methods. To illustrate its practical applicability, we use the methodology to detect structural changes in currency exchange rates in real time.
item.dc:creator: Per August Jarval Moen

item.title: Bayesian Variational Inference for Mixed Data Mixture Models
item.description: arXiv:2507.16545v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Heterogeneous, mixed type datasets including both continuous and categorical variables are ubiquitous, and enrich data analysis by allowing for more complex relationships and interactions to be modelled. Mixture models offer a flexible framework for capturing the underlying heterogeneity and relationships in mixed type datasets. Most current approaches for modelling mixed data either forgo uncertainty quantification and only provide point estimates, or use MCMC, which incurs a very high computational cost that is not scalable to large datasets. This paper develops a coordinate ascent variational inference algorithm (CAVI) for mixture models on mixed (continuous and categorical) data, which circumvents the high computational cost of MCMC while retaining uncertainty quantification. We demonstrate our approach through simulation studies as well as an applied case study of the NHANES risk factor dataset. We provide theoretical justification for our method by establishing that the CAVI variational posterior mean converges locally to the true parameter value and lies within $O(1/n)$ of the maximum likelihood estimator. Building on this result, we show that the CAVI variational posterior contracts around the true parameter at rate $n^{-1/2}$.
item.dc:creator: Junyang Wang, James Bennett, Victor Lhoste, Sarah Filippi

item.title: Inference with weights: Residualization produces short, valid intervals for varying estimands and varying resampling processes
item.description: arXiv:2507.19607v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Weighting is widely used in observational causal inference, yet basic questions remain about how to estimate the variance of weighted effect estimates. For example, when and how should sampling uncertainty in the weights be propagated into the final result? Should these weights reduce rather than inflate variance? Does the choice of weighted variance estimator depend on the target estimand and the assumed source of randomness? We show that a single, familiar estimator addresses these concerns across settings: robust standard errors from a weighted regression of the outcome on treatment, the centered balancing covariates, and their interaction with treatment. These residualized standard errors are valid and often substantially smaller than those from weighted regression on treatment alone, with reductions of up to 30% when covariates are prognostic. We establish their justification under design-based, model-based, and superpopulation frameworks, for both ATE and ATT estimands, and for exact balancing, approximate balancing, and inverse propensity weights. For inference to the superpopulation, we employ a simple correction. We further show that M-estimation yields nearly identical results when constructed to answer the same questions, and that the key issue is not "uncertainty in the weights" given a sample, but uncertainty over the sample. Simulations and three empirical applications confirm our analyses.
item.dc:creator: Erin Hartman, Chad Hazlett, Arisa Sadeghpour

item.title: Zeroes and Extrema of Functions via Random Measures
item.description: arXiv:2511.10293v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present methods that provide all zeroes and extrema of a function that do not require differentiation. Using point process theory, we are able to describe the locations of zeroes or maxima, their number, as well as their distribution over a given window of observation. The algorithms in order to accomplish the theoretical development are also provided, and they are exemplified using many illustrative examples, for real and complex functions.
item.dc:creator: Athanasios Christou Micheas

item.title: Location--Scale Calibration for Generalized Posteriors
item.description: arXiv:2511.15320v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: General Bayesian updating replaces the likelihood with a loss scaled by a learning rate, but posterior uncertainty can depend sharply on that scale. We propose a simple post-processing that aligns generalized posterior draws with the asymptotic sampling distribution of a penalized estimator, yielding uncertainty quantification that is asymptotically invariant to the learning rate. We prove a total-variation normal approximation at an effective scale determined by a score central limit theorem, allowing sample-size-dependent prior factors, non-i.i.d. observations, and locally smooth convex penalties under model misspecification. Within this framework, we justify the open-faced sandwich adjustment (Shaby, 2014) and extend it from covariance rescaling to a location--scale calibration whose draws converge in total variation to the target for any learning rate. In our empirical illustration, calibrated draws maintain stable coverage, interval width, and bias over orders of magnitude in the learning rate and closely track frequentist benchmarks, whereas uncalibrated posteriors vary markedly.
item.dc:creator: Shu Tamano, Yui Tomo

item.title: Balancing Weights for Causal Mediation Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2512.09337v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes the average treatment effect into components that operate through intermediate variables and a component that does not. This paper studies weighting estimation of generalized mediation functionals, whose contrasts include natural direct and indirect effects, for any fixed finite number of causally ordered mediators. Inverse propensity score weights are vulnerable to (a) weight instability, because they are products of estimated probability ratios, and (b) finite-sample covariate and mediator imbalance, which can bias the estimator. We instead propose sequential balancing weights, which address (a) by minimizing weight dispersion and (b) by imposing exact balance. Stage one balances covariates between a treatment group and the full sample. Each later stage adds the next mediator and balances a treatment group against the preceding weighted group. A finite-sample bias decomposition of the augmented weighting estimator determines these variables and targets. When exact balance cannot be attained in a small sample, the procedure relaxes the balancing conditions by tolerances selected without using the outcome. Under the stated assumptions, the estimated weights converge at every stage to their population inverse-probability counterparts, with errors from preceding stages entering additively. We also establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency of the augmented weighting estimator, together with conditions for consistent variance estimation. In the main simulation design with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights outperform the compared methods in bias, root mean squared error, and coverage. In a small media-framing experiment with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights reduce the imbalance left by propensity-score weighting.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Kawato

item.title: No prior over nuisance parameters is required for credible intervals and Bayes factors
item.description: arXiv:2601.17621v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work shows that there are procedures that maintain the subjective Bayesian property of coherently informing decision making under uncertainty (i.e., if they tell you to take a certain bet, you should) without needing to assign a prior distribution over nuisance parameters, only over the parameter(s) of interest. We first carefully define this sense of 'credibility', and show that within this framework one can condition on any statistic of choice rather than only on the full dataset. This relaxation of credibility is a natural middle ground between Bayesian and frequentist statistics in the following sense: To a p% Bayesian credible set we should assign a p% belief after observing both the dataset and the interval, to p% frequentist sets we can generally only assign a p% belief before observing either the data or the interval, while to the statistical sets proposed here we can assign a p% belief after observing the set, but not necessarily after inspecting the full dataset ourselves. We then show that choosing a conditioning statistic whose distribution we know, or can bound, for each value of the parameter of interest leads to prior-free Bayes factors even for composite hypotheses, and to non-parametric credible sets with priors only over the parameter of interest. We derive such procedures for several (groups of) statistical problems. Particularly noteworthy is that any frequentist test gives a Bayes factor of the power over the size of the test, and that anytime-validity of E-process-based tests can be carried over to this Bayes factor.
item.dc:creator: Tim Ritmeester

item.title: Bayesian variable and hazard structure selection in the General Hazard model
item.description: arXiv:2602.03756v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The proportional hazards (PH) and accelerated failure time (AFT) models are the most widely used hazard structures for analysing time-to-event data. When the goal is to identify variables associated with event times, variable selection is typically performed within a single hazard structure, imposing strong assumptions on how covariates affect the hazard function. To allow simultaneous selection of relevant variables and the hazard structure itself, we develop a Bayesian variable selection approach within the general hazard (GH) model, which includes the PH, AFT, and other structures as special cases. We propose two types of g-priors for the regression coefficients that enable tractable computation and show that both lead to consistent model selection. We also introduce a hierarchical prior on the model space that accounts for multiplicity and penalises model complexity. To efficiently explore the GH model space, we extend the Add-Delete-Swap algorithm to jointly sample variable inclusion indicators and hazard structures. Simulation studies show accurate recovery of both the true hazard structure and active variables across different sample sizes and censoring levels. Two real-data applications are presented to illustrate the use of the proposed methodology and to compare it with existing variable selection methods.
item.dc:creator: Yulong Chen, Jim Griffin, Francisco Javier Rubio

item.title: Conflict Forecasting via Conformal Prediction for Markov Processes
item.description: arXiv:2604.25139v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether or not a country is at war, or experiencing escalating or deescalating levels of conflict, has massive ramifications on a country's national and foreign policy. Given a country's history of conflict, or lack thereof, future predictions about the war-status of a country are valuable information. In this paper, we present the use of conformal prediction on temporally-dependent data to obtain prediction sets of possible future conflict state-sequences. More specifically, we compare the results of conformal prediction to a likelihood-based prediction strategy when the data are assumed to come from a discrete-state Markov process. A point-prediction may not supply sufficient information because the penalty for a wrong prediction is extreme, and so we consider a machine learning alternative that gives valid uncertainty quantification and is robust to model misspecification. In the data analysis, we present real forecasts of conflict dynamics across multiple countries. Lastly, we assess the differences between the conformal and likelihood-based prediction sets applied to training data which fall under a pervasive edge-case, not discussed in existing literature.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Basarkar, Emmett B. Kendall, David Randahl, Jonathan P. Williams, Gudmund H. Hermansen

item.title: Improving Variance Estimation for Covariate Adjustment with Binary Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2605.06655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Covariate adjustment is a general method for improving precision when estimating treatment effects in randomized trials and is recommended by the FDA in its 2023 guidance when baseline variables are prognostic for the primary outcome. We focus on a method highlighted in that guidance called ``standardization" (or ``g-computation") for estimating the marginal treatment effect. We address the question of how to reliably estimate variance for binary outcomes when marginal outcome probabilities are close to 0 or 1. We propose an influence function-based leave-one-out cross-validated (IF-LOO) variance estimator for the standardized difference-in-means average treatment effect. Through simulation studies, we show that this estimator provides appropriate type-I error control and performs reliably in challenging settings where existing methods can yield inflated type-I error or fail entirely, such as when outcome events are rare or sample sizes are small. In addition to having desirable statistical properties, we derive a closed-form expression for the proposed estimator, enabling straightforward and reliable implementation by study statisticians. The robust finite-sample performance and ease of implementation suggest the IF-LOO variance estimator is a prudent default choice for standardization in clinical trials.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlyn Lee, Alex Ocampo, Courtney Schiffman, Michel Friesenhahn, Christina Rabe, Michael Rosenblum

item.title: Hierarchical Bayes meets hierarchical forecasting: A flexible framework for level-focused forecasts
item.description: arXiv:2606.23009v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decision-making in hierarchical systems requires probabilistic forecasts at all cross-sectional levels. Current hierarchical forecasting methods typically generate independent forecasts at each level and reconcile them post hoc to ensure coherence between upper and lower levels. Such post hoc corrections do not incorporate hierarchical structure or decision goals into the underlying parameter estimation. We propose a fully Bayesian hierarchical forecasting framework that shares information more effectively between and across levels than reconciliation alone. Our approach has the flexibility to softly penalise incoherence, subject to model specification, and to focus the global model and coherence update on hierarchical levels most relevant to decision outcomes. This yields parameter estimates that are focused towards the forecasting goals and capture the requirement for coherency, removing the need to estimate covariance matrices for multi-step forecasting horizons. We demonstrate improvements in predictive accuracy metrics on both simulated data and Australian domestic tourism forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Arwen Nugteren, Mahdi Abolghasemi, Kerrie Mengersen, Christopher Drovandi

item.title: stLMM: Bayesian Spatial and Space-Time Linear Mixed Models for Small-Area Ecological Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2607.02836v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ecological monitoring programs often need estimates for areas and periods with few observations. Data may be available as measurements at known locations, measurements identified only by area, or area summaries. These differences in spatial and temporal support require models that connect available observations to the quantities and reporting scales of interest. stLMM is an R package for Bayesian linear mixed models that addresses these needs through a common formula interface for grouped, temporal, point-referenced, areal, and space-time effects, including coefficients that vary across these supports. It accommodates individual measurements and direct estimates with sampling variances, and predicts at unsampled locations or reporting units. Ecological small-area estimation motivates the package, while its model components support broader ecological applications. A shared sparse-precision implementation underlies the model terms. Structured latent effects are collapsed during parameter updates, then recovered for fitted values, diagnostics, prediction, and posterior summaries. This gives users one posterior-draw workflow for propagating uncertainty from model fitting through prediction and aggregation. An illustrative simulation connects point-referenced observations, point observations by area, and direct area estimates to a common prediction target. Timing and memory measurements for larger versions of these settings illustrate how computational demands differ between point-referenced and areal models. The package is also demonstrated with a Washington county biomass example, using national forest inventory data and tree canopy cover to estimate county-year biomass means. An extended article series provides reproducible source code, data, diagnostics, and related model variants.
item.dc:creator: Andrew O. Finley

item.title: Multilevel network meta-regression for multistate models: Population-adjusted joint synthesis of progression and survival from individual and aggregate data
item.description: arXiv:2607.25120v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In network meta-analysis (NMA) of oncology time-to-event outcomes, there is growing recognition that progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) are better synthesized jointly than in separate analyses. The multistate NMA of Jansen et al. addresses this with a tri-state (stable, progressed, dead) Markov model fitted to aggregate survival curves. It cannot, however, adjust for imbalance in effect modifiers across trials, so its relative effects may be biased or not apply to the target population. Multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) resolves covariate imbalance by integrating an individual-level model over each aggregate study's covariate distribution, coherently combining individual participant data (IPD) and aggregate data (AgD); however, for time-to-event outcomes it has been developed only for a single endpoint. This paper introduces multilevel network meta-regression for multistate models (ML-NMR-MS), which embeds the ML-NMR integrated IPD-plus-AgD likelihood inside an illness-death multistate model. For IPD studies the full multistate likelihood over linked transitions is used; for AgD studies covariate-marginal state-occupancy probabilities are computed by quasi-Monte Carlo integration of the occupancies implied by the transition intensities over the reconstructed covariate distribution, and entered through a conditional-survival likelihood. The resulting population-adjusted joint PFS/OS treatment effects can directly parameterize a state-transition economic model. On an illustrative network, ML-NMR-MS resolves a treatment's joint effect into its component transitions, separating an effect on progression from an effect on post-progression survival, and produces conditional and marginal effects. Under correct specification, a simulation study with known truth shows negligible bias and near-nominal coverage for the population-adjusted treatment effects.
item.dc:creator: Jeroen P Jansen

item.title: Structure-based Transfer Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.08487v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transfer learning improves estimation in a target study using information from related sources. Classical transfer learning is typically data-based, requiring access to the source data or to a model fitted on them. Neither is available in many modern studies, as both are often proprietary or unreported. What can be transferred instead is structure: summarized information derived from a source, such as the supports of predictors, which is available and interpretable without access to the source data or model. The prevalence of the Large Language Model (LLM) provides a rich source of such structure information. However, data-based transfer learning can not well utilize it as accessing the data and model of the LLM is often infeasible. In this paper, we propose a novel transfer learning framework based on structure. In particular, we focus on linear model and aim to use supports generated by multiple agents, such as LLM, to improve estimation in the target study. Our procedure maps each support into the target parameter space, aggregates the results with data-driven weights, and applies a sparse correction against inaccurate supports. We establish interpretable conditions for retaining the target-only Lasso rate and for a faster convergence rate, together with minimax optimality under joint coverage. Simulations and a DNA-methylation application illustrate gains and robustness.
item.dc:creator: Ho Yi Alexis Ho, Xinzhou Guo, Shuoxun Xu

item.title: Comparing survival prediction models with sharp bounds on Brier-risk differences before local outcomes are available
item.description: arXiv:2610.09658v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hospitals may need to compare an existing survival prediction model with a candidate before outcomes in their own patients become available. We develop a procedure to support this comparison under explicit assumptions about between-cohort differences and to identify when judgment should be deferred. For two fixed predictors, we derive and prove closed-form sharp bounds on their difference in fixed-horizon Brier risk under bounded, profile-specific conditional survival log-odds shifts. Evaluating both predictors against the same unknown target outcomes yields intervals no wider than subtraction of separately bounded risks. Censoring-adjusted estimation and simultaneous bootstrap confidence envelopes distinguish candidate support, reference support, and deferred judgment. In simulations with a superior reference predictor, separate identified intervals were on average 2.5-2.6 times as wide as direct intervals. At a sensitivity bound of 0.2, correct reference support occurred in 24.8-83.5% of replications with direct identification versus 6.5-19.6% with separate-risk subtraction; incorrect candidate support with direct identification was at most 0.1%. Coverage was 0.88-0.95 with 30% or 50% censoring but fell to 0.79-0.86 under 70% censoring. Three public-data applications examined transfer between hospitals, across time, and between successive clinical studies. Across fixed configurations, separate identified intervals were 1.77-16.4 times as wide as direct intervals. In 100 repeated splits per application, only direct identification supported the candidate at a sensitivity bound of 0.2 in 29%, 11%, and 8% of splits, respectively. The procedure provides additional evidence for provisional model comparison while allowing judgment to be deferred; it complements external validation, with caution required when censoring compromises confidence-envelope coverage.
item.dc:creator: Won Gi Choi, Sun-Ho Kim, Min Soo Kim

item.title: Small area learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a novel learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop estimators with and without cross-fitting, accommodating low-complexity and flexible learners and unifying synthetic, model-based, and semi-supervised estimators. For area means, we establish a unified asymptotic theory for these estimator families, characterizing conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality and providing variance estimators and confidence intervals without prescribing a particular learning algorithm. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals clearly a bias-variance trade-off: partial residual correction in classical estimators can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to the misspecification of working models, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34%-49% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Katarzyna Reluga, Nicola Salvati, Setareh Ranjbar, Nikos Tzavidis, Mark van der Laan

item.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
item.description: arXiv:2610.16947v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Statistical data editing in official statistics must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. Exact minimum-change correction can be computationally demanding. This paper develops a general framework for structured data whose dependencies admit a normalized acyclic routing representation. It connects routing metadata and explicitly specified semantic edits to logical admissibility, violation diagnosis, and correction. Under stated record semantics, the generated Horn theory characterizes admissibility without materializing its deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the origin of each requirement and identify the variables that can affect a violation. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.
item.dc:creator: Pierpaolo Massoli

item.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.28910v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator and change the structural equations, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint and then evaluate the unchanged structural equations on that state. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.
item.dc:creator: Jose M. Pe\~{n}a

item.title: Two-sample inference for sequence-derived feature distributions from deep sequencing data
item.description: arXiv:2610.36503v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many biological contexts involve heterogeneous populations of related molecular variants within a single individual. For example, some viral infections such as HIV-1 exhibit substantial diversity within a single host. Advances in sequencing technology now make it possible to characterize such populations by generating up to thousands of genetic sequences from a biological sample. In many settings, each sequence can be mapped to a numeric feature, such as Hamming distance to a reference sequence. This collection of feature values defines a one-dimensional distribution that characterizes individual-level viral diversity. When comparing these features across independent groups, past analyses have typically reduced each individual's data to a single summary value, such as the mean or mode. We propose a framework that retains the full individual-level distribution as the object of analysis. Drawing on existing tools from distributional data analysis, our framework uses Wasserstein barycenters to summarize the observed individual-level distributions within groups into a single representative distribution. These group barycenters are then compared using differences in quantiles and tested for equality. A practical challenge is that the number of sequences obtained, known as sequencing depth, can vary across biological samples. Through simulation studies, we examine when low sequencing depth can distort inference and present practical strategies for addressing these issues. We then illustrate the framework using data from the HIV-1 Antibody Mediated Prevention efficacy trials and a human B cell receptor sequencing study of vaccine-elicited immune responses. By using the entire collection of sequences for each individual, our approach can reveal group differences that may be obscured by single-number summary analyses.
item.dc:creator: James Peng, Florian Stijven, Michal Juraska, Allan C. deCamp, Elena E. Giorgi, Linbo Wang, Peter B. Gilbert

item.title: Model Criticism via Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.37837v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many generative models are specified by how data are simulated. An observation is a deterministic transform $Y=G(\theta,X)$ of a draw $X$ from an assumed noise law, indexed by a structural parameter $\theta$. Such models cover discrete, continuous and functional data, as well as i.i.d. replicates of stochastic processes, but their likelihoods are often unavailable. We propose a simulation-based procedure that tests whether such a model fits the data and, when it does not, locates where it fails, without choosing a test statistic. The procedure splits the data in two and is formulated as a two-stage stochastic program. In the estimation stage, $\theta$ is fitted on the first block by minimizing a Wasserstein distance between the data and simulations from the model. In the recourse stage, $\theta$ is frozen at the fitted $\tilde{\theta}$, and a finite set of representative noise values $\{\bar x_j\}$ is pushed through the fitted mechanism to give model atoms $G(\tilde{\theta},\bar x_j)$. The held-out block optimizes weights $\textbf{w}$ on the model atoms to best match its own distribution. The optimized weights are then compared with theoretical weights under correct specification. Since each model atom is the image of known noise values, the disagreement between optimal and theoretical weights points to the part of the noise law that is wrong. The split makes the scaled weights conditionally multinomial, yielding a calibrated Pearson test. We prove strong consistency of both stages under checkable assumptions and illustrate the procedure on a Gaussian location--scale family, the number of segregating sites under Kingman's coalescent, a Yule process, and an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion.
item.dc:creator: Ren-Yi Wang

item.title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.04366v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: at least 50% of the observational causal studies we review in leading journals state or imply it, while 7% describe an imputation model. We develop a framework for when complete-case regression consistently estimates the population average treatment effect (ATE). With a constant unit-level treatment effect, two checks suffice: whether covariates and the missingness indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools within-covariate comparisons appropriately, possibly using inverse propensity weighting. A collider--mediator illustration highlights the first check: the same missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism can require different adjustment choices. With heterogeneous effects, conditional effects must be transportable to the population and be reweighted to its population distribution. These formal results provide practical checks for applied researchers to run complete case regressions, recover existing guidance as special cases, and are illustrated with applications across fields.
item.dc:creator: Wenxin Lin, Shiyao Liu

item.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
item.description: arXiv:2611.09429v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite broad potential impact of selection bias it is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct selection bias, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle, applicability, limitations and data requirements. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R and prepares input for the external SPREG software. It provides worked examples using simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with open methodological challenges.
item.dc:creator: Ciarrah-Jane S Barry, Tahereh Gholipourshahraki, Zolt\'an Kutalik, Bjarni J Vilhj\'almsson, Esben Agerbo

item.title: Convergence and global optimality of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for Gaussian mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2611.14428v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study explicit Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for fitting Gaussian location mixtures by nonparametric maximum likelihood. The full sequence converges weakly and has finite length in the bounded-Lipschitz metric throughout the original step-size range. These conclusions hold for any fixed data set in any dimension and any initial probability measure. By an earlier conditional optimality theorem, the limit maximizes the likelihood under full-support initialization. Fix any particle step size in $(0,1]$. Initialize the particles by resampling the observations. For an open set of triples of points in the plane, the probability of convergence to a strictly suboptimal fixed point tends to one exponentially as the particle count grows. Without reweighting, a centered Gaussian initialization can give a strictly suboptimal limit. Every finite iterate has a smooth, strictly positive density. The limit assigns positive mass to a nonglobal local maximum of the associated Gaussian sum. We also give the exact pure-transport limit for a one-dimensional initialization with full support and an atom. An exact finite-dimensional representation preserves the truncated likelihood moments and the retained region's contribution to the current dissipation. This lets us transfer an analytic gradient inequality to the measure trajectory.
item.dc:creator: Xingzhou Wang, Ziyang Jiang, Zheng Li, Mingyan Liu, Yiling Wang, Jingze Yang

item.title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.14457v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised. We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to na\"ive KM risks. The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.
item.dc:creator: Ferran Espuny-Pujol

item.title: Testing the number of common factors by bootstrapped sample covariance matrix in high-dimensional factor models and errata
item.description: arXiv:2202.06188v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper studies the impact of bootstrap procedure on the eigenvalue distributions of the sample covariance matrix under a high-dimensional factor structure. We provide asymptotic distributions for the top eigenvalues of bootstrapped sample covariance matrix under mild conditions. After bootstrap, the spiked eigenvalues which are driven by common factors will converge weakly to Gaussian limits after proper scaling and centralization. However, the largest non-spiked eigenvalue is mainly determined by the order statistics of the bootstrap resampling weights, and follows extreme value distribution. Based on the disparate behavior of the spiked and non-spiked eigenvalues, we propose innovative methods to test the number of common factors. Indicated by extensive numerical and empirical studies, the proposed methods perform reliably and convincingly under the existence of both weak factors and cross-sectionally correlated errors. Our technical details contribute to random matrix theory on spiked covariance model with convexly decaying density and unbounded support, or with general elliptical distributions.
item.dc:creator: Long Yu, Peng Zhao, Wang Zhou

item.title: Prediction Sets and Conformal Inference with Interval Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2501.10117v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given data on a random variable $Y$, a prediction set with miscoverage level $\alpha \in (0,1)$ is a set that contains a new draw of $Y$ with probability at least $1-\alpha$. Among all prediction sets satisfying this coverage property, the oracle prediction set is the one with minimal volume. The oracle prediction set offers a complementary view of the distribution of $Y$, beyond point estimators such as the mean and quantiles, and has attracted considerable interest recently. This paper develops methods for estimating such prediction sets conditional on observed covariates when $Y$ censored or interval-valued. We characterise the oracle prediction set under partial identification induced by interval censoring and propose consistent estimators for both oracle prediction intervals and more general oracle prediction sets consisting of multiple disjoint intervals. In addition, we apply conformal inference to construct finite-sample valid prediction sets for interval outcomes that remain consistent as the sample size grows, using a conformity score tailored to interval data. The proposed procedure accounts for irreducible prediction uncertainty due to the stochastic nature of outcomes, modelling uncertainty arising from partial identification, and sampling uncertainty that vanishes as sample size increases. We conduct Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications using UK job postings data and the US Current Population Survey. The results demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Weiguang Liu, \'Aureo de Paula, Elie Tamer

item.title: Empirical Bayes Estimation in Heterogeneous Coefficient Panel Models
item.description: arXiv:2601.07059v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop an empirical Bayes (EB) G-modeling framework for short-panel linear models with nonparametric prior for the random intercepts, slopes, dynamics, and non-spherical error variances. We establish identification and consistency of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) under general conditions, and provide low-level sufficient conditions for several models of empirical interest. Conditions for regret consistency of the EB estimators are also established. The NPMLE is computed using a Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flow algorithm adapted to panel regressions. Using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, we find that the slope coefficient for potential experience is substantially heterogeneous and negatively correlated with the random intercept, and that error variances and autoregressive coefficients vary considerably across individuals. The EB estimates reduce mean squared prediction errors relative to individual maximum likelihood estimates.
item.dc:creator: Myunghyun Song, Sokbae Lee, Serena Ng

item.title: Calibeating Prediction-Powered Inference
item.description: arXiv:2604.21260v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study semisupervised mean estimation with a small labeled sample, a large unlabeled sample, and a black-box prediction model whose output may be miscalibrated. A standard approach in this setting is augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) [Robins et al., 1994], which protects against prediction-model misspecification but may be inefficient when the prediction score is poorly aligned with the outcome scale. We introduce Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, which post-hoc calibrates the prediction score on the labeled sample before using it for semisupervised estimation. This simple step requires no retraining and can calibeat the original score, improving it both as a predictor of the outcome and as a regression adjustment for semisupervised inference. We study both linear and isotonic calibration. For isotonic calibration, we establish first-order optimality guarantees: isotonic post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency relative to the original score and simpler post-processing rules, while replacing the fitted isotonic score by its conditional-mean oracle yields no additional first-order variance reduction. For linear calibration, we show first-order equivalence to PPI++. We also clarify the relationship between existing estimators, showing that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization [Rubin and van der Laan, 2008]. In simulations and real-data experiments, our calibrated estimators often outperform PPI and are competitive with, or outperform, AIPW and PPI++. We provide an accompanying Python package, ppi_aipw, at https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/.
item.dc:creator: Lars van der Laan, Mark Van Der Laan

item.title: A Practical Guide to Instrumental Variables Methods with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
item.description: arXiv:2605.15115v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Instrumental variables (IV) methods are central to applied microeconomics. While classical approaches assume linear models with constant effects, recent literature has shifted toward the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework to accommodate heterogeneous treatment effects. This paper provides a practical guide to aligning empirical practice with recent theory. We first examine how different specifications with covariates lead to distinct weighted averages of covariate-specific LATEs. We then discuss how parametric misspecification can undermine the causal interpretation of these estimands and suggest flexible specifications as essential robustness checks. Finally, we review formal tests for LATE assumptions and methods robust to monotonicity violations. We provide a guide to software implementations to help researchers apply the methods in practice.
item.dc:creator: Tymon S{\l}oczy\'nski, Liyang Sun, S. Derya Uysal

item.title: Hierarchical Projection for Adaptive Knowledge Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2606.08691v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transfer learning aims to improve estimation in a target population with limited data by borrowing information from related external datasets, referred to as sources. However, heterogeneity in target-source relevance and predictor-outcome relationships can lead to negative transfer, where model performance is worse than using target data alone, particularly in high-dimensional settings with partially overlapping features. We propose Projection Transfer Learning (ProjectionTL), a Bayesian framework that integrates hierarchical modeling with adaptive posterior projection to enable selective knowledge transfer at both the source and feature levels. In the first stage, a source-guided hierarchical prior adaptively combines information from multiple sources using data-driven weights that capture their global alignment with the target. In the second stage, a weighted posterior-projection procedure induces sparsity by preferentially retaining features supported by stronger agreement between source and target signals. This two-stage framework distinguishes global source relevance from coordinate-specific transferability, allowing informative components to be retained while reducing the influence of heterogeneous or non-transferable signals. We establish theoretical guarantees for posterior contraction and model selection consistency under high-dimensional regularity conditions, without requiring all sources to be informative. Simulation studies and applications to Alzheimer's disease neuroimaging data demonstrate improved estimation accuracy, variable selection, and predictive performance compared with others, including settings with heterogeneous sources and block-wise missing modalities.
item.dc:creator: Samhita Pal, Tian Gu

item.title: Modeling inhomogeneous spatial point configurations with applications to replicated patterns in real-life waiting crowds
item.description: arXiv:2606.14532v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this article, we connect statistical inference for spatial point processes with the analysis of waiting pedestrian crowds through two interconnected contributions. First, on the methodological side we develop an inference procedure for semiparametric spatial point process models leveraging replicated spatial patterns, i.e., multiple approximately independent realizations from the same process. Second, we show that spatial point processes provide a suitable modeling framework for waiting pedestrians, capturing two key aspects: spatial inhomogeneity driven by location attractiveness and repulsive interactions between pedestrians. These two components are central to the inference problem itself, since spatial point process modeling hinges on disentangling background intensity from interaction. Although replicated spatial patterns are rare in point process literature, they are available here through a unique real-life pedestrian dataset, thereby directly linking the methodological development to the physical application. We use the proposed methods to fit and evaluate determinantal and Gibbs point processes in a simulation study and a real-world case study. Despite persistent challenges in decoupling the influences of inhomogeneity from interaction, these models are able to reproduce key empirical features of waiting pedestrians.
item.dc:creator: Lars Sickert Karam, Rui M. Castro, Maarten Schoukens, Alessandro Corbetta

item.title: Doubly robust estimation of direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
item.description: arXiv:2610.37049v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.
item.dc:creator: Martin Huber

item.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.01666v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Whether an action-conditioned world model responds to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. Taking biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model. A second failure arises whenever many sites share one action sequence, as in world models: the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into an e-value near zero, so a valid test loses its power although the effect is real. Tempering the score changes the bet, not the validity. The log e-value is concave in the tempering factor and zero at zero, so too small a factor costs little and too large a one can cost everything; every single factor we tried, estimated or tuned, failed in some setting, and mixtures over a fixed grid never did. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed by pooling; a tempered statistic, registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field (E = 1.1e10). In three registered tests on models trained by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units of a diffusion model, and reached the power bar in 10 of 26 Atari games under IRIS's token likelihood and 1 of 6 control tasks under TD-MPC2; mixtures fixed in advance reached it in 96 units, 24 games and 6 tasks. On recorded robot video with iVideoGPT the mixture rejected in 155 of 159 trajectories; the pooled test did not collapse there (143). Under exact nulls the statistics made 14 rejections in 26,664 tests.
item.dc:creator: Bowen Xu, Boyu Chen, Jiaying Li

item.title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.13219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Shi Bo, Jiaming Hu

item.title: Local Fr\'echet regression with polyspherical predictors: Uniform convergence rates and factor selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.13240v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study local Fr\'echet regression for responses taking values in a metric space and predictors on a product of spheres of possibly different dimensions. We propose local constant and local linear estimators with factor-specific bandwidths and establish uniform convergence rates. We select sphere factors by comparing cross-fitted prediction risks for the full and leave-one-factor-out models. The procedure consistently recovers the active factor set, and the selected local constant and local linear estimators attain the same uniform convergence rates as if the active factor set were known. For univariate Wasserstein responses supported on a common compact interval, the uniform rate holds without an entropy condition on the response space. Simulations with scalar and spherical responses and analyses of vessel speeds and drifter speed distributions illustrate the methods.
item.dc:creator: Chang Jun Im
